lesson.title: Build a rain gauge
lesson.subtitle: Measure rain in millimetres with a plastic bottle

video.title: Build a rain gauge
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Morning in Amina’s classroom, puddles outside the window. Two pupils face each other: one stretches his arms wide (a lot of rain), the other pinches her fingers together (only a little). Amina, in a headscarf, looks from one to the other, amused.
scenes.animation: Arms stretch, fingers pinch; quick push-in on Amina’s amused face.
scenes.narration: Musa says it rained a lot last night. Zainab says only a little. Both families farm, so it matters. Who’s right? Today we stop guessing.
scenes.sound: Dripping water; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated primary teacher in a headscarf, ink outlines. Simple classroom; no text on the walls.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the IoT track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: build a rain gauge from a plastic bottle — and measure rain in millimetres.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A flat square of ground fills with rain like a shallow tray; a ruler stands upright in the water. Then three arrows show water running off, soaking in and rising as vapour — each one crossed out.
scenes.animation: Water rises in 1 s; three arrows appear, then are crossed out 200 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Rainfall is measured in millimetres. Ten millimetres of rain means that, on flat ground, the water would stand ten millimetres deep — if none ran off, soaked in or dried up.
scenes.sound: Gentle rain; soft tick as each arrow is crossed out.
scenes.vids: Keep the ruler large and simple so it reads on a small screen. No words in the art.

scenes.visual: Two straight-sided containers stand in the same rain: a wide bucket and a narrow bottle. Both fill. A teal line runs across at the same water height in both, while the bucket clearly holds more water.
scenes.animation: Rain falls; water rises together in both; the teal level line draws across in 600 ms.
scenes.narration: So we measure depth, not amount. A wide bottle catches more water than a narrow one. But if both have straight sides, the water stands at the same depth in each.
scenes.vids: Make the equal water height very clear; hold the final frame for 3 seconds.

scenes.visual: Clean card on white with the IoT track chip. A simple bottle rain gauge icon with a funnel on top and a scale on its side.
scenes.animation: Gauge pops in; raindrops fall into the funnel.
scenes.narration: A rain gauge is a container that collects rain so you can measure its depth. And you can make one from a clear plastic bottle.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: Step by step on a desk: an adult’s hands cut a straight-sided bottle where the shoulder starts to curve and tape the edge; pupils drop in stones, pour water to cover them and mark a teal 0 line; they tape on a ruler strip; the cut top goes in upside down.
scenes.animation: Each step slides in, about 4 seconds each, with a small check pop at the end.
scenes.narration: Choose a bottle with straight sides. An adult cuts off the top where it starts to curve, and tapes the sharp edge. Add a few stones, then water just to cover them — mark that level zero. Tape a millimetre scale up from zero. Turn the top upside down to make a funnel.
scenes.sound: Soft snip, tape tear, pebble clinks, water pouring.
scenes.vids: Only adult hands hold the scissors or knife. Generic bottle with no label or brand.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor pops in at his science lab bench, holding up two bottles: one straight-sided, one with a narrow waist in the middle. Two answer cards drop in, one picture each.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I’ve got two bottles: one with straight sides, one with a narrow waist in the middle. Which makes the better rain gauge?
scenes.sound: Two gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The straight bottle gets a blue check badge. In the waisted bottle, a small amount of water shoots a long way up the scale through the narrow part, beside a cross badge.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: The straight-sided one. Where a bottle narrows, a little rain rises a long way up the scale, so the reading is too high. Straight sides keep every millimetre true.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: A schoolyard from above. A gauge icon tries three spots: under a tree (leaves catch the drops), at a roof edge (drips pour in), then the middle of the open field, where it settles with stones packed around its base.
scenes.animation: The gauge hops between spots, 1 s each; a cross pops on the first two, a check on the third.
scenes.narration: Now, where to put it. Choose open ground, well away from roofs, walls and trees. Trees block the rain. Roofs drip extra water in. Stand it upright and firm, with stones around it if it’s windy.
scenes.vids: Blue check for the right spot, never green. Keep the yard simple, with no signs or text.

scenes.visual: Close-up at 8 am by a clock: a pupil crouches so her eye is level with the water, reads the scale, writes in a notebook, then pours water out down to the 0 line. A small calendar flips through a week; the gauge is emptied, rinsed and refilled to 0.
scenes.animation: Clock hands tick to 8; water pours out; calendar pages flip quickly.
scenes.narration: Then the routine. Read it at the same time every day — say, 8 am — at eye level. Write the millimetres and the date. Then pour it back down to zero, so no rain is counted twice. Once a week, empty it fully and refill to zero, so mosquitoes can’t breed.
scenes.vids: Show the pupil’s eye clearly level with the water line. Notebook shows simple lines only.

scenes.visual: Amina stands in the schoolyard beside a big shady neem tree, goats grazing nearby. A pupil holds the gauge under the tree. Two answer cards bounce in: a thumbs-up and a thumbs-down.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My pupils want to put the gauge under the big neem tree, where it’s safe from goats. Good idea?
scenes.sound: Gentle tick; a distant goat bleat.
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight the thumbs-down.

scenes.visual: The thumbs-down card gets the check badge; leaves catch falling drops. The gauge moves to the open field, with a low ring of thorny branches well back from it. Then five icons line up: straight bottle, funnel, ruler, open field, clock.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Not a good idea — the leaves catch the rain. Choose an open spot, and keep goats away another way. Remember: straight sides, a funnel, a millimetre scale, open ground, same time every day.
scenes.vids: Hold the five icons for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Amina’s class outside: groups hold up their bottle gauges and compare 0 lines, then carry one gauge to an open corner of the field. A pupil draws a reading rota on the board. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Data in class’.
scenes.animation: Groups walk out; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: build one gauge together. Choose a spot as a class, and give each pupil a day on the reading rota. Next lesson, we’ll turn your readings into a chart.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: Which bottle makes a better rain gauge?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — straight sides keep every millimetre on the scale equal to a millimetre of rain.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — where a bottle narrows, a little rain rises a long way up the scale, so it reads too high.

checkpoints.prompt: Should the gauge go under a big shady tree, where it’s safe from goats?

options.text: No — the leaves will catch the rain

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — leaves catch some rain and drip it unevenly. Choose open ground and keep animals away another way.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — under a tree, leaves catch some of the rain, so the reading can’t be trusted. Choose open ground.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3-minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Build a rain gauge”. Style: flat illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a teal (#14b8a6) track accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Amina Bello, a primary teacher in a headscarf. Follow the script scene by scene: pupils argue about last night’s rain; rainfall measured in millimetres of depth; why a wide and a narrow bottle agree; building a bottle gauge with a zero line, scale and funnel; a quiz pause; placing it in open ground; the daily reading routine; a second quiz pause; recap; end with the class building one gauge. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
